In mathematics, the '''supersilver ratio''' is a  geometrical [[aspect ratio|proportion]], given by the unique real [[polynomial root|solution]] of the equation {{nowrap|{{math|1=''x''{{isup|3}} = 2''x''{{isup|2}} + 1}}.}} Its decimal expansion begins with {{math|{{val|2.2055694304005903|end=...}} }} {{OEIS|A356035}}.<!-- PLEASE DO NOT add additional digits to the value of ς in this equation; there is a long-standing consensus that additional digits do not add to understanding. Thank you.-->

The name ''supersilver ratio'' is by analogy with the [[silver ratio]], the positive solution of the equation {{math|1=''x''{{isup|2}} = 2''x'' + 1}}, and the [[supergolden ratio]].

==Definition==
[[File:Supersilver cuboid.svg |thumb|upright=1.28 |ς = {{sfrac|a+d|a}} = {{sfrac|a|b}} = {{sfrac|b|d−a}}. For b = 1 the boxes have volumes {{math|1=ς{{isup|3}} = ς{{isup|2}} + 1 (red) + ς{{isup|2}} (green).}}]]

Three quantities {{math|a > b > c > 0}} are in the supersilver ratio if <math display=block> \frac{2a+c}{a} =\frac{a}{b} =\frac{b}{c}\,.</math>
This ratio is commonly denoted {{tmath|\varsigma}}.{{efn |{{math|a + c {{=}} d}} in the vector image on the right.}}

Substituting <math> a=\varsigma \,b = \varsigma^2 c </math> in the first fraction gives
<math display=block> \varsigma =\frac{2\varsigma^2 c + c}{\varsigma^2 c}.</math> It follows that the supersilver ratio is the unique real solution of the [[cubic equation]] <math>\varsigma^3 -2\varsigma^2 -1 =0.</math>

The [[Minimal polynomial (field theory)|minimal polynomial]] for the reciprocal root is the depressed cubic <math>x^3 +2x -1,</math> thus the simplest solution with [[Cubic equation#Cardano's formula|Cardano's formula]],
<math display=block> \begin{align}
 w_{1,2} &=\left( 1 \pm \frac{1}{3} \sqrt{ \frac{59}{3}} \right) /2 \\
 1 /\varsigma &=\sqrt[3]{w_1} +\sqrt[3]{w_2} \end{align} </math>
or, using the [[Cubic equation#Trigonometric and hyperbolic solutions|hyperbolic sine]], <math display=block> 1 /\varsigma =-2 \sqrt\frac{2}{3} \sinh \left( \frac{1}{3} \operatorname{arsinh} \left( -\frac{3}{4} \sqrt\frac{3}{2} \right) \right).</math>

{{tmath|1 /\varsigma}} is the superstable [[Fixed-point iteration|fixed point]] of the iteration <math> x \gets (2x^3 +1) /(3x^2 +2).</math>

Dividing the defining trinomial <math>x^3 -2x^2 -1</math> by {{tmath|x -\varsigma}} one obtains <math> x^2 +x /\varsigma^2 +1 /\varsigma ,</math> and the [[Conjugate element (field theory)|conjugate elements]] of {{tmath|\varsigma}} are
<math display=block> x_{1,2} = \left( -1 \pm i \sqrt{8\varsigma^2 +3} \right) /2 \varsigma^2,</math>
with <math>x_1 +x_2 = 2 -\varsigma \;</math> and <math>\; x_1 x_2 =1 /\varsigma.</math>

Multiply the minimal polynomial by {{tmath|x}}, and rearrange the relation as <math>(x^2 +1)^2 =x+1.</math> This results in the iteration <math> x_{n+1} \gets \sqrt{-1 +\sqrt{\phantom{|} 1+x_n}} </math>, with initial value {{tmath|x_0 >0 }}, and the [[Nested radical#Infinitely nested radicals|continued radical]]&nbsp;<ref>{{OEIS|A272874}}</ref>
<math display=block> 1/\varsigma =\sqrt{-1 +\sqrt{1 +\sqrt{-1 +\sqrt{\phantom{|} 1 +\cdots}}}} </math>

Its counterpart is found by using polynomial {{tmath|f:z^3 +z^2 -z -2}}, which has real zero {{tmath|\varsigma -1}}.<ref>{{OEIS|A137421}}</ref> Multiply {{tmath|f}} by {{tmath|z-1}}, then <math>(z^2 -1)^2 =z-1,</math> and the corresponding iteration with {{tmath|z_0 >1 }} gives
<math display=block> \varsigma -1 =\sqrt{1 +\sqrt{-1 +\sqrt{1 +\sqrt{\phantom{|} -1 +\cdots}}}} </math>

===Supersilver Julia sets===
{{multiple image
| total_width = 320
| direction   = vertical
| image1      = SupersilverCartouche.jpg
| caption1    = Julia set (in black) of the map {{math|z ← {{sfrac|2 − z{{sup|2}}|z{{sup|2}} − 1}} }} with fixed point {{math|1=z{{sub|f}} = ς − 1}}.
| image2      = SupersilverCartouche_rec.jpg
| caption2    = Julia set of the map {{math|r ← {{sfrac|4 − r{{sup|2}}|r{{sup|2}} − 2}} }} with fixed point {{math|1=r{{sub|f}} = 2 / (ς − 1)}}.{{br}} {{br}} Both images are centred at critical point {{math|0}}. Critical value {{math|−2}} is on the left border, the negative pole is at the cross, and the real fixed point is on the right hand side.
}}
Both systems have linear [[Rate of convergence|convergence rate]] <math> \,\log_{10} \tfrac{4(\varsigma -1)}{\varsigma} =0.340...</math> In order to improve this constant, divide both sides of <math> z^3 =z(1-z) +2 \,\text{ by } z,</math> and substitute <math>1 /\varsigma =1 /(z+1) \,</math> for {{tmath|\, 2/z -z}}, resulting in the iteration <math> z_{n+1} \gets \sqrt{1 +\frac{1}{1 +z_n}},</math> and the continued reciprocal square root
<math display=block> \varsigma -1 =\sqrt{1 +\cfrac{1}{1+\sqrt{1 +\cfrac{1}{1+\sqrt{1 +\cfrac{1}{1 +\ddots}}}}}} </math>

For complex initial points {{tmath|z_0}} other than {{tmath|-1}} this method converges with linear rate <math> \,\log_{10} 2(\varsigma^2 +1) =1.069...,</math> provided the [[Square root#Square roots of negative and complex numbers|principal root]] is chosen at each step. If randomly either the principal root or its negative is picked, the [[Orbit (dynamics)|orbit]] of {{tmath|z_0}} is [[Attractor|attracted]] to a [[Curve#Topological curve|simple closed curve]], which is the [[Julia set]] {{tmath|J}} of the backward iteration <math> z_{n-1} \gets \frac{1}{z^2_n -1} -1.</math>

The [[Critical point (mathematics)|critical points]] {{tmath|z_c}} for which the derivative {{tmath|-2z /(z^2 -1)^2}} vanishes are {{tmath|0}} and {{tmath|-\infty}}. The latter is mapped into the right neighborhood of the [[Zeros and poles|pole]] {{tmath|1=z_p =-1}} and ''vice versa'', so {{tmath|\{-\infty,-1\} }} is the single attracting [[limit set]].

On {{tmath|J}}, the repelling [[Fixed point (mathematics)|fixed points]] {{tmath|z_f}} are the zeros of {{tmath|f}}, namely {{tmath|\varsigma -1}}, and <math> \left( -\varsigma \pm i\sqrt{\tfrac{7 -\varsigma^2}{\varsigma -1}} \right) /2\,</math> (the centers of the largest spirals in the left half of the image) with [[Stability theory#Stability of fixed points|divergence rate]] <math> \tfrac12 \log_{10} \tfrac{8}{\varsigma^2 +1} =0.067...</math> The first [[Image (mathematics)#Inverse_image|preimages]] of {{tmath| \varsigma -1 \,}} are {{tmath|1 -\varsigma}}, and the purely imaginary conjugates <math> \pm i\sqrt{ \varsigma^2 -1}.</math>

'''The counterpart''' of this system, with equal rate of convergence, is derived from <math> r^3 =r(2-r) +4 \,</math> with real root {{tmath| \frac{2}{\varsigma -1},}} numerically {{math|1.658967...}}<ref>{{OEIS|A348909}}</ref> Divide both sides by {{tmath|r}}, and substitute <math>2 /\,\varsigma(\varsigma -1) =2 /(r+1) \,</math> for {{tmath|\, 4/r -r}}, resulting in the iterations <math> r_{n+1} \gets \sqrt{2 +\frac{2}{1 +r_n}} \,</math> and <math>\, r_{n-1} \gets \frac{2}{r^2_n -2} -1.</math> The backward iteration has derivative {{tmath|-4r /(r^2 -2)^2}}, thus the critical points {{tmath|-\infty}} and {{tmath|0}} remain unchanged, and the attracting limit set is {{tmath| \{-2,0\} }}.

On the corresponding Julia set, the repelling fixed points <math> \left( -\varsigma -\tfrac{1}{\varsigma} \pm i\sqrt{(7 -\varsigma^2)(\varsigma -1)} \right) /2\,</math> have divergence rate as above. The preimages of {{tmath| \frac{2}{\varsigma -1} \,}} are {{tmath| \frac{2}{1 -\varsigma} }}, and the conjugates <math> \frac{\pm 2i}{\sqrt{ \varsigma^2 -1}}.</math>

==Properties==
[[File:SupersilverSquare_6.svg |thumb |upright=1.25 |Rectangles with aspect ratios {{math|ς−1}}, {{sfrac|ς|ς−1}}, and {{math|ς}} tile the square.]]

The growth rate of the average value of the n-th term of a random Fibonacci sequence is {{tmath|\varsigma - 1}}.<ref>{{OEIS|A137421}}</ref>

The defining equation can be written
<math display=block> \begin{align}
 1 &=\frac{1}{\varsigma -1} +\frac{1}{\varsigma^2 +1} \\
 &=\frac{1}{\varsigma} +\frac{\varsigma -1}{\varsigma +1} +\frac{\varsigma -2}{\varsigma -1}.\end{align} </math>

The supersilver ratio can be expressed in terms of itself as fractions
<math display=block> \begin{align}
(\varsigma -1)^2 &=\frac{\varsigma +1}{\varsigma} \\
 \varsigma &=\frac{\varsigma}{\varsigma -1} +\frac{\varsigma -1}{\varsigma +1} \\
 \varsigma(\varsigma -1) &=\varsigma +\tfrac{1}{\varsigma} =\frac{\varsigma +1}{\varsigma -1} \\
 \varsigma^2 -1 &=\varsigma +\frac{2}{\varsigma -1} =\frac{1}{\varsigma -2} -1.\end{align} </math>

Similarly as the infinite [[geometric series]]
<math display=block> \begin{align}
 \frac{\varsigma}{\varsigma -1} &=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \varsigma^{-n} \\
 \frac{\varsigma}{(\varsigma -1)^3} &=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \varsigma^{-2n} \\
 \frac{\varsigma}{2} &=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \varsigma^{-3n},\end{align} </math>

in comparison to the [[silver ratio]] identities
<math display=block> \begin{align}
 \frac{\sigma}{\sigma -1} &=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sigma^{-n} \\
 \frac{\sigma}{2} &=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sigma^{-2n} \\
 \frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma +3} &=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sigma^{-3n}.\end{align} </math>

For every integer {{tmath|n}} one has
<math display=block> \begin{align}
 \varsigma^n &=2\varsigma^{n-1} +\varsigma^{n-3} \\
 &=4\varsigma^{n-2} +\varsigma^{n-3} +2\varsigma^{n-4} \\
 &=\varsigma^{n-1} +2\varsigma^{n-2} +\varsigma^{n-3} +\varsigma^{n-4} \end{align}</math>
from this an infinite number of further relations can be found.

[[Simple continued fraction|Continued fraction]] pattern of a few low powers
<math display=block> \begin{align}
 \varsigma^{-2} &=[0;4,1,6,2,1,1,1,1,1,1,...] \approx 0.2056 \;(\tfrac{5}{24}) \\
 \varsigma^{-1} &=[0;2,4,1,6,2,1,1,1,1,1,...] \approx 0.4534 \;(\tfrac{5}{11}) \\
 \varsigma^0 &=[1] \\
 \varsigma^1 &=[2;4,1,6,2,1,1,1,1,1,1,...] \approx 2.2056 \;(\tfrac{53}{24}) \\
 \varsigma^2 &=[4;1,6,2,1,1,1,1,1,1,2,...] \approx 4.8645 \;(\tfrac{73}{15}) \\
 \varsigma^3 &=[10;1,2,1,2,4,4,2,2,6,2,...] \approx 10.729 \;(\tfrac{118}{11}) \end{align}</math>

As derived from its continued fraction expansion, the simplest rational approximations of {{tmath|\varsigma}} are:<math display=block>\tfrac{9}{4},\tfrac{11}{5},\tfrac{53}{24},\tfrac{75}{34},\tfrac{161}{73},\tfrac{236}{107},\tfrac{397}{180},\tfrac{633}{287},\tfrac{1030}{467},\tfrac{1663}{754},\tfrac{2693}{1221},\tfrac{7049}{3196}, \ldots</math>

[[File:Supersilver Newton map.svg |thumb|upright=1.25 |[[Newton's method]] for {{math|1=p(z) = z{{isup|3}} − 2z{{isup|2}} − 1:}} {{nowrap|{{math|ς}} (right)}} and its complex conjugates at the nuclei of their [[Attractor#Basins_of_attraction|basins of attraction]]. [[Julia set]] of the Newton map in orange, with unit circle and real curve for reference.]]

The supersilver ratio is a [[Pisot number]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Panju |first=Maysum |date=2011 |title=A systematic construction of almost integers |url=https://mathreview.uwaterloo.ca/archive/voli/2/panju.pdf |journal=The Waterloo Mathematics Review |volume=1 |issue=2 |pages=35–43}}</ref> By definition of these numbers, the [[Absolute value#Complex numbers|absolute value]] <math>1 /\sqrt{\varsigma}</math> of the algebraic conjugates is smaller than 1, so powers of {{tmath|\varsigma}} generate [[almost integer]]s.<ref>{{cite oeis|A332647|2=a(n) = 2*a(n-1) + a(n-3) with a(0) = 3, a(1) = 2, a(2) = 4}}</ref>
For example: <math> \varsigma^{10} =2724.00146856...</math> {{tmath|\approx 2724 +1/681}}. After ten rotation steps the [[Phase (waves)|phase]]s of the inward spiraling conjugate pair &ndash; initially close to {{tmath|\pm 45 \pi/82}} &ndash; nearly align with the imaginary axis.

The [[Minimal polynomial (field theory)|minimal polynomial]] of the supersilver ratio <math> m(x) =x^3 -2x^2 -1 </math> has [[discriminant]] <math>\Delta=-59</math> and factors into <math>(x -21)^{2}(x -19) \pmod{59};\;</math> the imaginary [[quadratic field]] <math> K = \mathbb{Q}( \sqrt{\Delta}) </math> has [[Binary quadratic form#Reduction and class numbers|class number]] {{tmath|h{{=}}3}}. Thus, the [[Hilbert class field]] of {{tmath|K}} can be formed by adjoining {{tmath|\varsigma}}.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/184423/ |title=Hilbert class field of a quadratic field whose class number is 3 |date=2012 |website=Mathematics stack exchange |access-date=May 1, 2024}}</ref>
With argument <math> \tau=(1 +\sqrt{\Delta})/2\, </math> a generator for the [[ring of integers]] of {{tmath|K}}, the real root [[J-invariant|{{math|&nbsp;<big>''j''(''τ'')</big>}}]] of the Hilbert class polynomial is given by <math>(\varsigma^{-6} -27\varsigma^{6} -6)^{3}.</math><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Berndt |first1=Bruce C.|last2=Chan |first2=Heng Huat |date=1999 |title=Ramanujan and the modular j-invariant |journal=[[Canadian Mathematical Bulletin]] |volume=42 |issue=4 |pages=427–440 |doi=10.4153/CMB-1999-050-1 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://fungrim.org/topic/Modular_j-invariant/ |title=Modular j-invariant |last=Johansson |first=Fredrik |date=2021 |website=Fungrim |access-date=April 30, 2024 |quote=Table of Hilbert class polynomials}}</ref>

The [[Weber modular function|Weber-Ramanujan class invariant]] is approximated with error {{math|< 3.5 ∙ 10<sup>−20</sup>}} by <math display=block>\sqrt{2}\,\mathfrak{f}( \sqrt{ \Delta} ) = \sqrt[4]{2}\,G_{59} \approx (e^{\pi \sqrt{- \Delta}} + 24)^{1/24},</math> while its true value is the single real root of the polynomial <math display=block>W_{59}(x) = x^9 -4x^8 +4x^7 -2x^6 +4x^5 -8x^4 +4x^3 -8x^2 +16x -8.</math>

The [[Modular lambda function#Lambda-star|elliptic integral singular value]]&nbsp;<ref>{{MathWorld |id=EllipticIntegralSingularValue |title=Elliptic integral singular value}}</ref> <math> k_{r} =\lambda^{*}(r) \text{ for } r =59 </math> has closed form expression
<math display=block> \lambda^{*}(59) =\sin ( \arcsin \left( G_{59}^{-12} \right) /2) </math>
(which is less than 1/294 the [[Eccentricity (mathematics)#Ellipses|eccentricity]] of the orbit of Venus).

==Third-order Pell sequences==
{{multiple image
| total_width=320
| direction=vertical
| image_gap=6
| image1=Supersilver_Rauzy_baa.png
| caption1=''Hop o' my Thumb'': a supersilver [[#matrix|Rauzy fractal]] of type {{nowrap|a ↦ baa.}} The fractal boundary has [[Minkowski–Bouligand dimension|box-counting]] [[Fractal dimension|dimension]] 1.22
| image2=Supersilver_Rauzy_bca.png
| caption2=A supersilver Rauzy fractal of type {{nowrap|c ↦ bca,}} with areas in the ratios {{math|ς{{sup|2}} + 1 : ς (ς − 1) : ς : 1.}}
}}

These numbers are related to the supersilver ratio as the [[Pell number]]s and [[Pell number#Pell–Lucas numbers|Pell-Lucas numbers]] are to the [[silver ratio]].

The fundamental sequence is defined by the third-order [[recurrence relation]]
<math display=block> S_n =2S_{n-1} +S_{n-3} \text{ for } n > 2,</math>
with initial values <math display=block> S_0 =1, S_1 =2, S_2 =4.</math>

The first few terms are 1, 2, 4, 9, 20, 44, 97, 214, 472, 1041, 2296, 5064,... {{OEIS|A008998}}.
The limit ratio between consecutive terms is the supersilver ratio:<math> \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} S_{n+1}/S_n =\varsigma.</math>

The first 8 indices n for which {{tmath|S_n }} is prime are n = 1, 6, 21, 114, 117, 849, 2418, 6144. The last number has 2111 decimal digits.

The sequence is extended to negative indices using <math display=block> S_n =S_{n+3} -2S_{n+2},</math>
obtaining (1), 0, 0, 1, 0,−2, 1, 4,−4,−7,12,10,...

Powers of the supersilver ratio can be written with third-order Pell numbers as quadratic coefficients <math display=block> \varsigma^n =\varsigma^2 S_{n-2} +\varsigma S_{n-4} +S_{n-3},</math> which is proved by [[mathematical induction]] on {{tmath|n}}. This relation also holds for {{tmath|n < 0}}. The order of the coefficients corresponds to the bottom row of matrix {{tmath|Q}} below.

The [[generating function]] of the sequence for non-negative {{tmath|n}} is given by&nbsp;<ref>{{OEIS|A008998}}</ref> <math display=block> \frac{1}{1 -2x -x^3} =\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} S_n x^n \text{ for } x <\tfrac{1}{\varsigma} </math>

The third-order Pell numbers are related to sums of [[binomial coefficient]]s by&nbsp;<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mahon |first1=Br. J. M. |last2=Horadam |first2=A. F. |date=1990 |title=Third-order diagonal functions of Pell polynomials |journal=[[The Fibonacci Quarterly]] |volume=28 |issue=1 |pages=3–10|doi=10.1080/00150517.1990.12429513 }}</ref> <math display=block> S_n =\sum_{k =0}^{\lfloor n /3 \rfloor}{n -2k \choose k} \cdot 2^{n -3k} </math>

The [[Characteristic equation (calculus)|characteristic equation]] of the recurrence is <math> x^3 -2x^2 -1 =0 .</math> If the three solutions are real root {{tmath|\varsigma}} and conjugate pair {{tmath|\beta}} and {{tmath|\gamma}}, the supersilver numbers are given by the [[Fibonacci sequence#Binet's formula|Binet formula]]
<math display=block>S_{n-1} =a \varsigma^n +b \beta^n +c \gamma^n ,</math>
with real {{tmath|a}} and conjugates {{tmath|b}} and {{tmath|c}} the roots of <math> 59x^3 -6x -1 =0.</math>

Since <math> \left\vert b \beta^n +c \gamma^n \right\vert < \varsigma^{-n/2} </math>, the number {{tmath|S_n }} is the [[nearest integer function|nearest integer]] to {{tmath| \,a\,\varsigma^{n+1} }}, with {{tmath|n \ge 0}} and coefficient <math> a =\varsigma^2 /(\varsigma^3 +2) =</math> {{gaps|0.38215|95259|06012|16354|62213...}}

Coefficients <math> a =b =c =1 </math> result in the Binet formula for the related sequence <math> A_n =S_n +2S_{n-3}.</math>

The first few terms are 3, 2, 4, 11, 24, 52, 115, 254, 560, 1235, 2724, 6008,... {{OEIS|A332647}}.

This third-order Pell-Lucas sequence has the [[Fermat's little theorem|Fermat property]]: if p is prime, <math> A_{p} \equiv A_1 \bmod p.</math> The converse does not hold, but the small number of odd [[pseudoprime]]s <math>\,n \mid (A_n -2) </math> makes the sequence special. The 14 odd composite numbers below {{math|10{{sup|8}} }} to pass the test are n = 3{{sup|2}}, 5{{sup|2}}, 5{{sup|3}}, 315, 99297, 222443, 418625, 9122185, 3257{{sup|2}}, 11889745, 20909625, 24299681, 64036831, 76917325.<ref>Only one of these is a 'restricted pseudoprime' as defined in: {{cite journal |last1=Adams |first1=William |last2=Shanks |first2=Daniel |author-link2=Daniel Shanks |title=Strong primality tests that are not sufficient |journal=[[Mathematics of Computation]] |publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] |date=1982 |volume=39 |issue=159 |pages=255–300 |doi=10.1090/S0025-5718-1982-0658231-9 |doi-access=free| jstor=2007637}}</ref>

[[File:Supersilver_Rauzy_aba.png |thumb|upright=1.25 |''The Pilgrim'': a supersilver Rauzy fractal of type {{nowrap|a ↦ aba.}} The three subtiles have areas in ratio {{math|ς.}}]]

The third-order Pell numbers are obtained as integral powers {{math|''n'' > 3}} of a [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] with real [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors#Eigenvalues and eigenvectors of matrices|eigenvalue]] {{tmath|\varsigma}} <math display=block> Q = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} ,</math>

<math display=block id="matrix"> Q^n = \begin{pmatrix} S_n & S_{n-2} & S_{n-1} \\ S_{n-1} & S_{n-3} & S_{n-2} \\ S_{n-2} & S_{n-4} & S_{n-3} \end{pmatrix} </math>

The [[Trace (linear algebra)#Relationship to eigenvalues|trace]] of {{tmath|Q^n }} gives the above {{tmath|A_n}}.

Alternatively, {{tmath|Q}} can be interpreted as [[incidence matrix]] for a [[Morphic word#D0L system|D0L]] [[L-system|Lindenmayer system]] on the alphabet {{tmath|\{a,b,c\} }} with corresponding  [[Semi-Thue system|substitution rule]]
<math display=block>\begin{cases}
a \;\mapsto \;aab \\
b \;\mapsto \;c \\
c \;\mapsto \;a \end{cases}</math>
and initiator {{tmath|w_0{{=}}b}}. The series of words {{tmath|w_n}} produced by iterating the substitution have lengths <math> l(w_n) =S_{n-2} +S_{n-3} +S_{n-4}.</math><ref>for n &ge; 2 {{OEIS|A193641}}</ref> The number of {{math|''c'', ''b'' and ''a's''}} in each word is equal to successive third-order Pell numbers.

Associated to this string rewriting process is a [[Compact space|compact]] set composed of [[Self-similarity|self-similar]] tiles called the [[Rauzy fractal]], that visualizes the [[Combinatorics on words|combinatorial]] information contained in a multiple-generation three-letter sequence.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Siegel |first1=Anne |last2=Thuswaldner |first2=Jörg M. |date=2009 |title=Topological properties of Rauzy fractals |url=http://numdam.org/item/MSMF_2009_2_118__1_0/ |journal=Mémoires de la Société Mathématique de France |volume=118 |series=2 |pages=1–140 |doi=10.24033/msmf.430}}</ref>

==Supersilver rectangle==
[[File:Supersilver ratio.svg |thumb|upright=1.5 |Powers of {{math|ς}} within a supersilver rectangle.]]

Given a rectangle of height {{math|1}}, length {{tmath|\varsigma}} and diagonal length <math>\varsigma \sqrt{\varsigma -1}.</math> The triangles on the diagonal have [[Altitude (triangle)|altitudes]] <math>1 /\sqrt{\varsigma -1}\,;</math> each perpendicular foot divides the diagonal in ratio {{tmath|\varsigma^2}}.

On the right-hand side, cut off a square of side length {{math|1}} and mark the intersection with the falling diagonal. The remaining rectangle now has [[aspect ratio]] <math>1 +1/ \varsigma^2:1</math> (according to <math>\varsigma =2 +1/ \varsigma^2</math>). Divide the original rectangle into four parts by a second, horizontal cut passing through the intersection point.<ref>Analogue to the construction in: {{cite journal |last=Crilly |first=Tony |date=1994 |title=A supergolden rectangle |journal=[[The Mathematical Gazette]] |volume=78 |issue=483 |pages=320–325 |doi=10.2307/3620208|jstor=3620208 }}</ref>

The parent supersilver rectangle and the two scaled copies along the diagonal have linear sizes in the ratios <math>\varsigma:\varsigma -1:1.</math> The areas of the rectangles opposite the diagonal are both equal to <math>(\varsigma -1)/ \varsigma,</math> with aspect ratios <math>\varsigma(\varsigma -1)</math> (below) and <math>\varsigma /(\varsigma -1)</math> (above).

If the diagram is further subdivided by perpendicular lines through the feet of the altitudes, the lengths of the diagonal and its seven distinct subsections are in ratios <math>\varsigma^2 +1:\varsigma^2:\varsigma^2 -1:\varsigma +1:</math> <math>\, \varsigma(\varsigma -1):\varsigma:2/(\varsigma -1):1.</math>

===Supersilver spiral===
[[File:Supersilver_spiral.svg |thumb |upright=1.5 |Supersilver spirals with different initial angles on a {{math|ς}}− rectangle.]]
A supersilver spiral is a [[logarithmic spiral]] that gets wider by a factor of {{tmath|\varsigma}} for every quarter turn. It is described by the [[polar equation]] <math>r( \theta) =a \exp(k \theta),</math> with initial radius {{tmath|a}} and parameter <math>k =\frac{2}{\pi} \ln( \varsigma).</math> If drawn on a supersilver rectangle, the spiral has its pole at the foot of altitude of a triangle on the diagonal and passes through vertices of rectangles with aspect ratio <math>\varsigma(\varsigma -1)</math> which are perpendicularly aligned and successively scaled by a factor {{tmath|\varsigma^{-1} }}. The pole of the spiral divides the diagonal of the lower right rectangle in ratio {{tmath|\varsigma}}.


==See also==
Solutions of equations similar to <math>x^3 =2x^2 +1</math>:
* [[Silver ratio]] – the positive solution of the equation <math>x^2 =2x +1</math>
* [[Golden ratio]] – the positive solution of the equation <math>x^2 =x +1</math>
* [[Supergolden ratio]] – the real solution of the equation <math>x^3 =x^2 +1</math>
